source.title: A Solvable Model of Adaptive Learning Rate Rescaling: Acceleration, Stability&Scaling
source.authors: Itay Lavie; Clarissa Lauditi; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. There are minor PDF/OCR artifacts in equations and figure text, but the content is intelligible.
record.tranche_reason: Extends loss-scaling analysis to normalized SGD and image-classification experiments, reporting how loss changes over training time and compute in that setting.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or total compute, nor does it test predictions from small language-model runs. Its relevant results concern loss decay over optimization time in a power-law random-feature model and linearized image models, including finite-step breakdown of the predicted acceleration.
record.test_reason: Weak, indirect test. The paper is a theory of normalized-SGD dynamics in a solvable random-feature model. Its only result on real networks is linearized (kernel-regime) ResNets on CIFAR-5M. There, held-out MSE falls as a power law in images seen and compute, then bends to a shallower SGD exponent when the effective learning rate hits marginal stability. That bears loosely on V5 (power-law form in an image setting) and V7 (an optimizer-dependent exponent and a bend away from a single power law). The random-feature derivations and simulations are the study's own toy-model theory, not measurements of the versions' systems.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that normalized SGD accelerates the transient loss decay, but at finite step size the growing effective learning rate ends this, via width-limited, EoSS or EoS phases. These phases govern when larger batches or wider models save steps at similar compute. Linearized-ResNet CIFAR-5M experiments support the acceleration, its breakdown, and the batch- and width-dependent compute trends.
record.recipe_differences: Studies normalized SGD in a power-law random-feature model and linearized ResNets, focusing on training-time dynamics, stability, batch size, and width rather than language-model cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss dynamics depend on teacher and data spectral exponents, finite step size and stability cutoff, width, and batch size. The CIFAR-5M experiment uses exponents measured from the infinite-width NTK and target alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: In a power-law random-feature model, normalized SGD maps the gradient-flow time exponent r_SGD to 2r_SGD/(1−r_SGD) for a < 1/2. It gives exponential decay at a = 1/2 and finite-time convergence for a > 1/2. Finite-step stability then ends the acceleration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer update-norm normalization changes the time-scaling exponent of loss, while leaving width- and data-limited exponents unchanged, until a stability cutoff.

fits_no_version.finding: In CIFAR-5M linearized ResNets, the smallest batch and the narrowest width were the most compute-efficient for the measured spectral exponents, as the theory predicts (Sec. VI, Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute efficiency of batch size and width (steps saved per unit compute) depends on data and target spectral exponents and on the stability phase.

record.problems: Evidence for the image-model experiments is described qualitatively in the text and figures; two seeds per cell are reported, but no uncertainty intervals are stated. The experiments use linearized networks in the lazy/kernel regime and do not establish scaling for language-model pretraining.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports detailed batch- and width-efficiency analyses for its normalized-SGD setup, but these do not measure the parameter/token/compute scaling laws named by V1–V3.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; the width and batch efficiency analyses concern steps to a target loss, not the loss-optimal N–D split.
No depth/width shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No feature-learning (non-linearized) image models, video, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. No loss-vs-model-size frontier across widths fitted as a power law.
No comparison of published LM laws, parameter-counting conventions or fitting methods.

missing.what: Width and batch compute-efficiency result on CIFAR-5M (narrowest width and smallest batch compute-optimal); no row records it, and rows_left_out describes only the theory analyses.
missing.locator: Sec. VI; Fig. 5 left and right

record.verdict_notes: Marginal relevance to the scaling-law claim. The paper uses neural scaling-law theory (spectral random-feature models) as a framework to study optimizer dynamics. Its time-exponent results are toy-model derivations, so rows R1–R4 are relinked to none. Only R5 (real linearized networks) bears, weakly, on V5 and V7. It is a kernel-regime image classifier and shows per-run learning curves rather than a compute-optimal frontier, so labels are tentative. No quantitative fitted exponents or error bars are reported for the experiments.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter-count and token-count allocation sweep.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests normalized-SGD training dynamics in a power-law random-feature model and linearized ResNets on CIFAR-5M. Does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or whether parameter/token/compute scaling laws generalize to other modalities.
No downstream-task performance prediction from pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting methods or parameter-count conventions for published scaling-law exponents, or test disagreement between Kaplan and Hoffmann allocation laws.

rows.subject: power-law random-feature model
rows.size_stated: Proportional limit d, N, B → ∞ at fixed width and batch ratios ν := N/d and α := B/d; Fig. 1 uses large α and ν = 10.
rows.operation_detail: Derives normalized-SGD loss decay over training time in the continuous-time limit.
rows.measure: Loss decay exponent over physical training time
rows.note: The derived loss is a power law in time for a < 1/2; the paper describes it as accelerated relative to matched-initial-update-norm SGD.
rows.check: Analytical continuous-time derivation in a toy power-law random-feature model. No language, image or video model is measured. It shows how normalization rescales the time exponent, not whether model loss follows a power law in parameters, data or compute. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: power-law random-feature model
rows.size_stated: Proportional limit d, N, B → ∞ at fixed width and batch ratios ν := N/d and α := B/d.
rows.operation_detail: Derives normalized-SGD loss decay over training time in the continuous-time limit.
rows.measure: Loss decay form over physical training time
rows.baseline: Ordinary SGD has power-law exponent r_SGD = 1 in the τ clock
rows.value: Exponential loss convergence, L(t) ∼ e^(−2√b t)
rows.note: This is a distinct teacher-exponent regime; the loss is not a power law in physical time.
rows.check: Toy-model derivation for the a = 1/2 regime (exponential decay in time). It is not a measurement of any version's system. The 'partial' state is meaningless here.

rows.subject: power-law random-feature model
rows.size_stated: Proportional limit d, N, B → ∞ at fixed width and batch ratios ν := N/d and α := B/d.
rows.operation_detail: Derives normalized-SGD loss convergence over training time in the continuous-time limit.
rows.measure: Loss convergence form over physical training time
rows.baseline: Ordinary SGD has power-law exponent r_SGD > 1 in the τ clock
rows.note: This regime gives formal finite-time convergence rather than a power law in physical time.
rows.check: Toy-model derivation for the a > 1/2 regime (formal finite-time convergence). It is not a measurement of any version's system.

rows.subject: power-law random-feature model
rows.size_stated: Large but finite α and ν; Fig. 1 gives ν = 10.
rows.operation_detail: Compares finite-step normalized-SGD dynamics with the continuous-time loss prediction and identifies the stability cutoff.

conditions.value: before and after t_stab, when η_eff reaches 2/λ_max

rows.baseline: Continuous-time normalized-SGD prediction before t_stab; standard SGD power-law scaling after the cutoff
rows.value: Simulations and DMFT track the accelerated prediction for t < t_stab; after the stability threshold, acceleration breaks down and the dynamics enter the stability-controlled regime.
rows.note: The paper explicitly says finite-step stability ultimately interrupts the accelerated loss decay.
rows.check: Simulations and DMFT of the random-feature model showing finite-step stability breaking the accelerated decay (Fig. 1). This is optimizer-stability behaviour in a toy model, not a scaling-law measurement on a real system.

rows.subject: linearized ResNets on CIFAR-5M
rows.size_stated: Width sweep w = 4 to 256; batch sweep B = 10 to 10,000; two seeds per cell.
rows.operation_detail: Trains normalized-SGD linearized networks and compares loss decay with predicted accelerated and post-stability scaling.
rows.measure: Held-out mean-squared error over training steps and compute
rows.baseline: Predicted transient exponent 2r_SGD/(1 − r_SGD) = 0.21, followed by standard SGD exponent after the effective learning rate reaches marginal stability
rows.value: The authors report that the experiments support the predicted accelerated loss decay and its crossover toward SGD-like scaling.
rows.uncertainty: Two seeds per cell; no error bar or confidence interval stated.
rows.note: The main text reports the result qualitatively; held-out performance is MSE, not language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: Linearized ResNets on CIFAR-5M, single pass, B = 2 to 10,000 (Appendix G; the record says 10), w = 4 to 256, two seeds per cell (241 runs). The comparison is to predicted exponents (0.21 transient, then r_SGD = 0.095) shown as rulers on Fig. 5; no fitted exponents or uncertainty are reported. For V5: power-law segments appear in an image setting, but only in a lazy/kernel regime and as a broken power law (partial). For V7: the bend from one exponent to another, set by optimizer stability, is reported (observed). The baseline field mixes the theory prediction with a baseline.

relationships.condition: Linearized ResNets (kernel regime) on CIFAR-5M with normalized SGD, single pass
relationships.reason: Held-out MSE follows power-law segments in images seen and compute, but the exponent switches at marginal stability, so no single power law holds; evidence is qualitative (rulers on Fig. 5). R5.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out MSE showed qualitative power-law segments against images seen and compute, with an exponent change at marginal stability.

relationships.condition: Same CIFAR-5M linearized-ResNet setting, normalized SGD versus SGD-like late phase
relationships.reason: The loss-curve exponent depends on the optimizer (0.21 accelerated versus 0.095 SGD) and the curve bends where the effective learning rate saturates. This is shown qualitatively on Fig. 5. R5.
relationships.display_finding: The loss exponent was 0.21 in the accelerated phase versus 0.095 for SGD, and the curve bent where the effective learning rate saturated.
